prompt.context: Our client, Hudson Bank, is an online bank that plans to launch a new credit card product within the next six months. They have asked us to help them determine a pricing model that will maximize their revenues.
prompt.question: What pricing model should Hudson Bank adopt for their new credit card product in order to maximize revenues?

clarifying_info.q: What customer segments does Hudson Bank target?
clarifying_info.a: Two core segments: Transactors (pay off entire balance each month) and Revolvers (carry a balance month to month).

clarifying_info.q: How does Hudson Bank generate revenue from the credit card?
clarifying_info.a: Three ways: 1) Merchant Fee, 2) Annual Percentage Rate (APR), and 3) Annual Fee.
The cost structure is the same regardless of pricing strategy, so focus on revenues.

clarifying_info.q: What other products does Hudson Bank offer?
clarifying_info.a: Hudson Bank offers other lending products such as personal and student loans, but the sole focus is their new credit card product.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape like?
clarifying_info.a: Competition is very strong in this space, so finding the right pricing strategy is critical.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average loan/credit card balance?
clarifying_info.a: The anticipated average annual credit card balance is $5,000.

clarifying_info.q: What is the merchant fee rate?
What are the typical transaction amounts and frequency?
clarifying_info.a: Forecasted average transaction amount is $100 with an expectation of 25 swipes per customer in the first year.

clarifying_info.q: Can we adjust the annual fee?
clarifying_info.a: No — annual fees cannot be adjusted because these funds cover operational costs for servicing each customer.

clarifying_info.q: Can we adjust the merchant fee?
clarifying_info.a: No — merchant fees will not be adjusted in order to balance Hudson Bank's merchant acceptance rate with the competitive landscape.

clarifying_info.q: Are there expected growth rates beyond the first year?
clarifying_info.a: Our client is most interested in the first twelve months following the credit card launch.

exhibits.title: Forecasted Customer Demand by APR
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing forecasted number of customers (in thousands) for Transactors and Revolvers at four APR levels: 10%, 15%, 20%, and 25%.

framework: Customers: Understand the two target segments (Transactors vs. Revolvers) and their price sensitivity; consider loyalty programs (cash back, referral) to grow the base
Competition: Benchmark industry APR ranges, annual fees, and merchant fees to understand competitive pricing boundaries
Company: Assess Hudson Bank's risk appetite (prime vs. sub-prime lending) and potential for cannibalization of existing financial products (personal/student loans)
Technology: Evaluate long-term scalability of onboarding new customers onto the credit card platform
Regulatory environment: UDAAP/CFPB restrictions on pricing strategies, especially any tiered or segment-specific models
Revenue streams: Quantify and optimize each stream — APR revenue, annual fee, merchant fees, late fees — across the demand curve

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, what do you notice about how the two customer segments respond to different APR levels? What does this imply for pricing strategy?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate should observe that Transactors are relatively price inelastic (demand stays flat from 10%–20%, holding at 4,500–5,000), while Revolvers are highly price elastic (demand drops sharply from 8,000 at 10% to 2,700 at 25%). This implies the APR choice will disproportionately affect Revolver volume and APR revenue. The candidate should also note that both segments must be priced on the same APR model to mitigate regulatory risks during the first year, and that the exhibit forecasts only the first year after launch.

questions.prompt: Using the data provided, calculate total expected annual revenue (Annual Fee + APR + Merchant Fee) at each APR level and determine the revenue-maximizing APR.
questions.guidance: The candidate should build a structured table across four APR levels. Key insight: 25% APR can be quickly ruled out due to sharply lower Revolver demand. A strong candidate proceeds methodically through each revenue stream before summing. Optimal APR is 20% at $6.425M. A secondary acceptable answer is 15% ($6.39M) because it is close in revenue, brings 1,600 more customers, and poses lower default risk in downturns.

math.setup: For each APR level: (1) Convert segment units to actual customers (×1,000). (2) Annual Fee Revenue = Total Customers × $100. (3) APR Revenue = # Revolvers × $5,000 avg balance × APR (Transactors contribute $0 since they pay off monthly). (4) Merchant Fee Revenue = Total Customers × $100 avg transaction × 25 swipes × 2%. (5) Total Revenue = sum of steps 2–4.
math.answer: Optimal APR = 20%, generating $6,425,000 in Year 1 revenue from 9,500 customers. Note: 15% APR generates $6,390,000 from 11,100 customers and is a defensible alternative.

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors should Hudson Bank consider before finalizing their pricing strategy?

categories.name: Optimal APR risk considerations
ideas: A 20% APR creates higher risk of customer default during economic downturns; 15% APR generates nearly the same revenue with meaningfully lower default risk
The revenue forecast covers only Year 1 and does not account for changes in consumer preferences or customer growth trajectory
Competitors offering lower APRs, no annual fees, or lower merchant fees may capture market share and make Hudson Bank's card hard to acquire

categories.name: Customer acquisition and retention
ideas: Introduce cash-back bonuses or customer loyalty programs to grow the new cardholder base (note: current market trend strongly favors rewards cards)
Promote lower APRs to cross-sell customers who already hold a personal or student loan with Hudson Bank to incentivize adoption
Develop strategies to increase average transaction volume or swipe frequency for Transactors, since APR revenue does not apply to them

categories.name: Regulatory and strategic considerations
ideas: Customizing pricing by customer segment (different APR for Transactors vs. Revolvers) could maximize revenue further but raises UDAAP/CFPB regulatory concerns — a tiered model may be feasible in Year 2 after validating compliance
Define a clear 'top of wallet' strategy: what will make customers prefer this card over competitors for daily spending?
Evaluate how the new credit card interacts with Hudson Bank's existing personal and student loan products to avoid cannibalization

recommendation: Recommend setting the APR at 20%, which is projected to attract 9,500 customers and generate $6.425M in Year 1 revenue — the highest of the four options modeled
An equally defensible recommendation is 15% APR, which generates $6.39M (only $35K less) from 1,600 more customers, offering greater volume and lower credit risk in a potential economic downturn
risks: A 20% APR carries higher default risk, particularly for Revolvers, if economic conditions deteriorate
The pricing model is uniform across segments due to regulatory constraints in Year 1, which may leave revenue on the table from price-insensitive Transactors
Revenue forecast covers only Year 1 and does not incorporate growth, churn, or competitive response
Strong competition from cards with lower APRs, rewards programs, or no annual fees could limit customer acquisition
next_steps: Conduct sensitivity analysis on Revolver default rates at 20% APR to size the credit loss exposure
Model Year 2+ revenue projections incorporating expected customer growth and competitive dynamics
Evaluate feasibility and regulatory pathway to a segment-differentiated pricing model in Year 2
Design a loyalty/rewards program to improve customer acquisition and 'top of wallet' positioning
Assess cross-sell opportunity: offer lower APR to customers already holding Hudson Bank loans
